hero.title: Welcome to <highlight>Taíno Nation of Borikén</highlight>
hero.subtitle: Reconnect with your ancestral roots, preserve your lineage, and join a sovereign community dedicated to honoring our Indigenous heritage and cultural identity.

heritage.label: About Our Platform
heritage.title: Preserving <highlight>Heritage</highlight> Through Technology
heritage.subtitle: The Taíno Nation Digital Platform is a sovereign, community-owned system designed to honor our ancestors, preserve our lineage, and strengthen our bonds as Indigenous descendants of Borikén.

sovereignData.title: Sovereign Data
sovereignData.description: Your data belongs to you. You maintain ownership and control over the personal information and files you upload to your account. You may also choose to contribute selected files to the tribally governed “Indigenous Archives of Puerto Rico” project, where they will become part of a communally held archive stewarded for cultural preservation, kinship research, and future learning by Borikua Taíno community members.

culturalIdentity.title: Cultural Identity
culturalIdentity.description: Receive your official Tribal ID, trace your maternal lineage, and connect with your ancestral Yucayeke to strengthen your Indigenous identity.

communityHelp.title: Community Help
communityHelp.description: Learn from and contribute to a growing community resource hub where members can share information related to health services, legal assistance, job searches, cultural events, and other support for Taíno Nation members.

mission.title: Our Mission
mission.body: To create a secure, culturally grounded digital platform that empowers Borikua Taíno descendants to reclaim their heritage, document their lineage, and participate in a thriving Indigenous community. We honor the wisdom of our ancestors while embracing modern technology to ensure our culture, traditions, and identity endure for generations to come.

process.label: Enrollment Process
process.title: How to Enroll with the Taíno Nation of Borikén
process.subtitle: Our enrollment process is designed to be simple, respectful, and thorough. Follow these steps to begin your journey toward official tribal membership.

prerequisite.label: Before you start
prerequisite.description: Create your account and verify your email address. Once you sign in and accept the enrollment consents, the five steps below open in your dashboard.

1.description: Provide your basic details — name, date of birth, contact information, and addresses.

2.description: Document your mother and maternal grandparents with names, dates, and places of birth.

3.description: Document your father and paternal grandparents the same way.

4.description: Upload your photo, proof of identity, and any records that support your kinship claim.

5.description: Review everything, sign, and submit your application for council review.

yucayeke.label: Yucayeke Regions
yucayeke.title: Connect to Your Ancestral Land
yucayeke.subtitle: Each enrolled member is assigned to a Yucayeke, a traditional land-based community that connects you to your ancestral territory and fellow descendants from your region.

overview.mapAlt: Illustrated map of Boriken representing Yucayeke regions
overview.title: What is a Yucayeke?
overview.paragraph1: In Taíno culture, a Yucayeke was a village or settlement led by a cacique. These communities were organized around territories throughout Borikén, each with its own identity, traditions, and leadership.
overview.paragraph2: Today, we honor this tradition by assigning members to historical Yucayeke regions based on their maternal lineage and ancestral connections. This helps preserve our territorial heritage and strengthens bonds within regional communities.

faq.label: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.title: Questions About Enrollment?
faq.subtitle: Find answers to common questions about the enrollment process, membership benefits, and platform features.

eligibility.question: Who is eligible to enroll in the Taíno Nation?
eligibility.answer: Taíno descendants who can provide personal identification and documentation supporting their maternal and paternal kinship are eligible to begin the enrollment process. If you are still gathering records, you can review the requirements first and prepare your materials before submitting.

timeline.question: How long does the enrollment process take?
timeline.answer: The enrollment application typically takes 20 to 30 minutes to complete. After submission, our review team carefully examines your application and supporting documents. The full review process usually takes 4 to 6 weeks, and you will receive status updates along the way.

security.question: Is my personal information secure?
security.answer: Yes. Personal information is encrypted and stored on secure sovereign servers. Access is limited to authorized reviewers involved in the enrollment process, and your data is not shared with third parties.

benefits.question: What benefits do enrolled members receive?
benefits.answer: Enrolled members can access their Tribal ID, document their maternal and paternal kinship, connect with their assigned Yucayeke, use the secure document vault, and explore member services such as health, legal, educational, and community support resources.

fee.question: Is there a fee to enroll?
fee.answer: No. There is no fee to begin the enrollment application. What you will need most is time to complete the form accurately and supporting documents to help verify your lineage.

Northwest coastal region known for rich fishing traditions, maritime heritage, and strong community bonds. Your maternal lineage connects you to this ancestral territory.

welcome.title: Welcome to Guainía
paragraphs: Guainía was one of the most prominent coastal Yucayeke regions in pre-colonial Borikén, strategically positioned along the northwest shores. This region was known for its skilled fishermen, expert canoe builders, and thriving maritime trade networks that connected communities across the Caribbean.

The people of Guainía developed sophisticated fishing techniques, sustainable coastal management practices, and maintained strong spiritual connections to the ocean. Today, descendants from this region continue to honor these traditions while building modern community bonds.
welcome.mapAlt: Illustrated topographic map of the Guainía coastal region

maritime.title: Maritime Heritage
maritime.description: Deep connection to ocean traditions, fishing practices, and coastal stewardship.

trade.title: Trade Networks
trade.description: Historical hub for inter-island commerce and cultural exchange across the Caribbean.

community.description: Active member network with regular gatherings, cultural events, and shared support.

legacy.description: Understanding the rich history and cultural significance of your ancestral territory.

preColonial.title: Pre-Colonial Era (Before 1493)
preColonial.description: Guainía was established as one of the principal Yucayeke regions under the leadership of respected caciques. The community thrived through sustainable fishing practices, advanced agricultural techniques in coastal valleys, and extensive trade networks with neighboring islands. Archaeological evidence shows sophisticated settlement patterns, ceremonial plazas, and evidence of complex social organization.

colonial.title: Colonial Period (1493-1898)
colonial.description: During Spanish colonization, the Guainía region experienced significant upheaval. Many Taíno people were forced into encomienda labor systems, yet communities maintained cultural practices through resistance and adaptation. Coastal settlements became strategic locations for maritime activities, and Indigenous knowledge of local waters proved invaluable. Despite attempts at cultural erasure, maternal lineages preserved traditions, language fragments, and spiritual practices in secret.

modern.title: Modern Revival (1900s-Present)
modern.description: The 20th and 21st centuries have seen a powerful resurgence of Taíno identity in the Guainía region. Descendants have reconnected through genealogical research, cultural education programs, and community organizing. Today, Guainía members actively participate in language revitalization efforts, traditional craft workshops, ceremonial gatherings, and advocacy for Indigenous rights. The digital platform has enabled unprecedented connection among regional members.

aymaco.description: Northwestern territory around present-day Aguadilla and Aguada, seat of cacique Aymamón — one of the confirmed yucayekes of the contact era.

abacoa.description: Territory of cacique Arasibo along the Río Grande de Arecibo, spanning roughly from Quebradillas to Arecibo.

sibuco.description: North-coast territory on the Río Cibuco around present-day Vega Baja, led by cacique Guacabo.

toa.description: Fertile lands of the Río Toa near Vega Alta and Dorado under cacique Aramaná, an early center of cassava cultivation.

bayamon.description: Territory of cacique Majagua in the Bayamón river basin, covering present-day Bayamón and the Toa Alta–Toa Baja region.

guaynabo.description: Attributed to cacique Mabó around present-day Guaynabo. Early records are debated, so it is held as oral tradition pending further research.

hamanio.description: Territory of Yuisa of Loíza, one of the few recorded female caciques of Borikén, at the mouth of the Río Grande de Loíza.

canaibon.description: Lands of cacique Canóbana along the Río Canóvanas, around present-day Canóvanas and Río Grande.

dacuao.description: Eastern territory around Naguabo and Ceiba, recorded as Daguao in the early chronicles.

macao.description: Southeastern territory of cacique Humacao, whose name survives in the present-day municipality.

guayaney.description: Southeastern coastal territory of cacique Guaraca, around present-day Patillas and Maunabo.

guayama.description: Southern territory of cacique Guamaní, around present-day Guayama and Salinas.

guania.description: Seat of the paramount cacique Agüeybaná, spanning the southwest from Cabo Rojo toward Ponce — the most influential cacicazgo of Borikén at the time of contact.

yaguecax.description: Western territory of cacique Urayoán in the Yagüez river valley, around present-day Mayagüez and Añasco.

otao.description: Mountain heartland of cacique Guarionex around Utuado and Lares, home to major ceremonial centers of the cordillera.

guajataca.description: Territory linked to cacique Mabodamaca around Quebradillas and Isabela — preserved chiefly through oral tradition while historical confirmation is pending.

jatobonico.description: Central mountain territory of cacique Orocobix along the upper Río Jatibonico, around Orocovis, Barranquitas, and Coamo.

turabo.description: Territory of cacique Caguax in the Turabo valley — present-day Caguas carries his name.

bieque.description: The island territory of Vieques and Culebra, remembered for cacique Cacimar, who led resistance from the offshore islands.

hayuya.description: Mountain territory of cacique Hayuya in the present-day Jayuya region, where the toponym persists — held as oral tradition pending confirmation.

loquillo.description: Northeastern territory associated with cacique Loquillo near the Luquillo range — held as oral tradition pending confirmation.
